decks.title: Directing — Part 1: Meaning, Principles, Supervision and Motivation
goals: Explain the meaning, characteristics and importance of directing
Apply the principles of directing to business situations
Describe the role of a supervisor
Explain motivation and identify needs using Maslow's hierarchy

slides.heading: Directing
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what **directing** is, its **principles**, **supervision** and **motivation**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what directing is, its characteristics and importance, the principles of directing, supervision, and motivation with Maslow's hierarchy
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: A factory can have excellent plans, a neat organisation chart and well chosen staff, and still nothing happens until someone tells people what to do, guides them and keeps them keen. That is directing. In this part we see what directing means, why it matters, the principles that guide it, the role of the supervisor, and how people are motivated.

slides.heading: Four elements of directing
slides.body_md: **Directing** means instructing, guiding, motivating, leading and communicating with people so that they work towards the goals of the organisation.

visual.alt: Diagram with directing in the centre, linked to its four elements: supervision to oversee and guide work, motivation to stir the will to work, leadership to influence people, and communication to share ideas and orders
visual.caption: The four elements of directing.

slides.narration: Directing has four elements. Supervision is overseeing the work and guiding people on the job. Motivation stirs their willingness to work. Leadership is the ability to influence them. Communication carries ideas, orders and feedback between people. A manager uses all four together, every day, to turn plans into results.

slides.heading: Characteristics of directing

rows: Work actually starts only when people are directed
Every manager directs those below, from chief executive to supervisor
It never stops while the organisation exists

visual.alt: Table of four characteristics of directing: it initiates action, takes place at every level, is a continuous process, and flows from top to bottom

slides.narration: Note four characteristics. Directing initiates action, because the other functions only prepare for work. It happens at every level, since every manager has people to guide. It is continuous, going on as long as the organisation exists, whoever holds the posts. And it flows from the top downwards, from superiors to subordinates.

slides.heading: Why directing matters

rows: Many people pull in one direction

visual.alt: Table of the importance of directing: it initiates action, integrates efforts, brings out potential, eases change and gives stability and balance

slides.narration: Directing is often called the heart of management. It starts action. It integrates the efforts of many people so that they pull in one direction. Good guidance draws out people's abilities. When a firm changes its methods, directing helps people accept the change. And it brings stability and balance, so that the firm can grow steadily.

slides.heading: Principles of directing (1)

rows: Draw out the full potential of every employee
Personal goals in line with company goals
Pick the method that suits the people and situation

visual.alt: Table of the first four principles of directing: maximum individual contribution, harmony of objectives, unity of command, and appropriateness of direction technique, each explained in a line

slides.narration: Experience has given managers a set of principles for directing. The first four are these. Get the maximum contribution from each person. Keep personal goals in harmony with the firm's goals. Give each subordinate only one boss, which is unity of command. And choose a direction technique that suits the people and the situation, because no single method works everywhere.

slides.heading: Principles of directing (2)

rows: Instructions must be clear and understood
Work with the groups that exist anyway
Influence people without weakening their goodwill
Check how orders are carried out and help

visual.alt: Table of the next four principles of directing: managerial communication, use of informal organisation, leadership, and follow through, each explained in a line

slides.narration: Four more principles complete the list. Communication from managers must be clear so that orders are understood. Informal groups exist in every firm, so managers should use them rather than fight them. Managers should lead, influencing people without hurting their goodwill. Finally, follow through: after giving an order, check how it is being carried out and help where needed.

slides.heading: Quick check: which principle?
slides.body_md: A paint company changes its sales commission so that staff gain most when the company gains most.
slides.narration: Ask whose goals are being brought together here, and the principle will be clear.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: spotting principles in a case
slides.body_md: Match each line from an imagined courier hub to the principle it shows.
bullets: Step 1 — Read each line and ask what problem it solves.
Step 2 — One boss for each rider: unity of command.
Step 3 — Rewards that rise with the firm's gains: harmony of objectives.
Step 4 — Checking on day one: follow through; working through a team captain: informal organisation.

headers: Line from the case (imagined courier hub, Vizag)
rows: Riders now get route orders only from the hub lead
A rider who cuts fuel use shares in the saving
The hub lead rides along on day one of the new route
Changes are first explained to the riders' cricket-team captain

visual.alt: Worked example table for an imagined courier hub in Vizag: orders only from the hub lead shows unity of command; sharing fuel savings shows harmony of objectives; riding along on day one shows follow through; briefing the cricket-team captain shows use of informal organisation

slides.narration: Let us practise on an imagined courier hub in Vizag. Riders taking route orders only from the hub lead shows unity of command. A rider sharing in the fuel he saves shows harmony of objectives. The hub lead riding along on the first day of a new route shows follow through. Explaining changes first to the cricket captain uses informal organisation. In exams, quote the line, then name the principle.

slides.heading: Supervision and the supervisor
slides.body_md: **Supervision** is overseeing what subordinates are doing and guiding them so that work is done as planned. The supervisor is at the operational level.

nodes.label: Supervisor: carries problems and ideas back up

visual.alt: Flow showing the supervisor between management and workers: management plans, the supervisor explains and guides, workers do the work, and the supervisor carries problems and ideas back up
visual.caption: The supervisor as a link

slides.narration: Supervision means overseeing subordinates at work and guiding them. The supervisor sits at the lowest level of management, closest to the workers. He or she explains plans to workers, trains and guides them, keeps the group united, and carries their problems and suggestions back to management. That is why the supervisor is often called the link between management and workers.

slides.heading: Quick check: what is the supervisor doing?
slides.body_md: A shift supervisor at a printing press shows a new operator how to set the colour rollers.
slides.narration: Think about which job of the supervisor is about teaching skills at the workplace.

slides.heading: Motive, motivation and motivator

rows: An inner urge that moves a person to act
The process of stirring people to act towards goals
A tool a manager uses to motivate

visual.alt: Table of three terms: a motive is an inner urge, motivation is the process of stirring people to act towards goals, a motivator is a tool such as a bonus or promotion

slides.narration: Three related words. A motive is an inner urge, such as the wish to own a scooter. Motivation is the process of stirring people to act towards goals. A motivator is a tool a manager uses, such as a bonus or a promotion. Motivation is an internal feeling, it can be positive or negative, and it is complex because people differ.

slides.heading: The motivation process

visual.alt: Flow of the motivation process: unsatisfied need, tension, drive, search behaviour, need satisfied, tension reduced
visual.caption: How motivation works

slides.narration: Motivation starts with an unsatisfied need. The need creates tension, the tension creates a drive, and the drive leads to search behaviour, that is, action to satisfy the need. When the need is satisfied, the tension falls. Managers can use this chain by offering rewards that meet the needs their employees actually feel.

visual.caption: Maslow's need hierarchy.

slides.narration: Abraham Maslow arranged human needs in five levels. At the bottom are physiological needs such as food and shelter, met at work by basic pay. Next come safety needs, then affiliation or belonging. Above those are esteem needs, for status and respect. At the top is self-actualisation, the urge to become everything one is capable of becoming.

slides.heading: Quick check: climb the hierarchy
slides.body_md: Put the five needs in order from the lowest to the highest.
slides.narration: Start with what a person needs simply to survive, and end with reaching one's full potential.

slides.heading: Assumptions of Maslow's theory
bullets: People's behaviour depends on their **needs**.
Needs follow an **order** from lower to higher.
A **satisfied need no longer motivates**; the next higher need takes over.
A person moves up only when the lower need is **reasonably met**.
slides.narration: The theory rests on a few assumptions. Behaviour depends on needs. Needs follow an order, from basic to higher. Once a need is satisfied it stops motivating, and the next higher need becomes the driver. So a manager should first find out where an employee stands, and then offer something that meets the next unmet need.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: identifying needs
slides.body_md: Four employees of an imagined dairy plant in Erode ask for different things. Name each need.
bullets: Step 1 — Find the words that show what the person lacks.
Step 2 — Survival items point to physiological; permanence points to safety.
Step 3 — Friends and groups point to affiliation; names and titles point to esteem.

rows: An advance for his family's groceries
To join the staff football team
Her method named in the plant manual

visual.alt: Worked example table for an imagined dairy plant in Erode: a new helper wanting an advance for groceries shows a physiological need; a contract worker wanting a permanent post shows a safety need; a transferred worker wanting to join the football team shows affiliation; a chemist wanting her method named shows esteem

slides.narration: Look at the four employees. Murugan wants an advance for groceries, a basic survival need, so physiological. Lakshmi wants a permanent post, which is about security, so safety. Joseph wants to join the football team, which is about belonging, so affiliation. Revathi wants her method named in the manual, which is about respect, so esteem.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false?
slides.body_md: Only top-level managers perform the function of directing.
slides.narration: Think about the supervisor on the shop floor. Does he or she guide anyone?

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Instructing, guiding, motivating, leading and communicating
Initiates action, every level, continuous, top to bottom
Eight, from maximum contribution to follow through
Overseeing work; the supervisor links management and workers
Five needs; a satisfied need stops motivating

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: the meaning of directing, its features, eight principles, supervision and the supervisor as a link, and Maslow's five needs

slides.narration: To sum up: directing sets people in motion through supervision, motivation, leadership and communication. It initiates action, happens at every level, is continuous and flows downward. Eight principles guide it. The supervisor oversees work and links management with workers. Motivation starts from unsatisfied needs, and Maslow arranges those needs in five levels, from physiological to self-actualisation.

slides.heading: Exam tips
slides.body_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling "one boss" harmony of objectives: it is **unity of command**.
- Confusing **esteem** (status, recognition) with **self-actualisation** (full potential).
- Writing that only top managers direct.

**How marks are awarded**
- Case parts: quote the line **and** name the principle or need.
- 5 marks: five clear points of about 20 words each.

rows: Need named and the words that reveal it
One point per mark, each with a short reason

visual.alt: Table of exam tips: to identify a principle, quote the line and name it; to identify a need, name it and quote the revealing words; to explain importance, give one point per mark with a reason

slides.narration: A few tips. Read each case line slowly and match it to exactly one principle or need. Esteem is about respect and status; self-actualisation is about growing to one's full potential. Remember that directing happens at every level. In case questions, marks come for quoting the line and naming the concept, so do both every time.

decks.title: Directing — Part 2: Incentives, Leadership and Communication
goals: Classify financial and non-financial incentives with examples
Explain the importance of leadership and the qualities of a good leader
Choose a suitable leadership style for a situation
Explain the communication process, its forms and barriers, and ways to improve it

slides.heading: Directing: incentives, leadership and communication
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **incentives**, **leadership** and **communication**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: financial incentives, non-financial incentives, leadership and its styles, the communication process, and barriers with remedies
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we look at the tools a manager uses while directing. First, incentives, both financial and non-financial. Then leadership: why it matters, what makes a good leader, and the main styles. Finally communication: how it works, formal and informal channels, the barriers that block it, and how to remove them.

slides.heading: Incentives: two kinds

rows: Money or benefits with money value

visual.alt: Table comparing financial incentives, which are money or benefits with money value and mainly satisfy lower needs, with non-financial incentives, which have no direct money value and mainly satisfy higher needs

slides.narration: An incentive is anything that encourages people to work better. Financial incentives are in money or have a money value, such as a raise or a pension. They mainly meet lower needs. Non-financial incentives have no direct money value, such as recognition or a challenging job. They mainly meet higher needs. A good manager uses both.

slides.heading: Financial incentives

rows: Extra pay per carton above target
A share of the year's profit
Shares at a price below market

visual.alt: Table of seven financial incentives with imagined examples: pay and allowances, productivity-linked wages, bonus, profit sharing, co-partnership or stock options, retirement benefits, and perquisites

slides.narration: Here are the main financial incentives. Pay and allowances, such as a yearly raise. Productivity-linked wages that reward higher output. A bonus over the wage. Profit sharing, where staff get part of the profit. Co-partnership or stock options, where staff can buy shares cheaply. Retirement benefits like provident fund and pension. And perquisites such as a car or housing.

slides.heading: Non-financial incentives

rows: A whole product to make, not one step
Freedom to decide on the spot

visual.alt: Table of eight non-financial incentives with imagined examples: status, organisational climate, career advancement, job enrichment, employee recognition, job security, employee participation and employee empowerment

slides.narration: Non-financial incentives include status, a friendly and fair organisational climate, chances of career advancement, and job enrichment, which makes work more varied and challenging. Recognition, job security, participation in decisions and empowerment, which means freedom to decide, also motivate strongly. They matter most once pay is reasonable.

slides.heading: Quick check: match the incentive
slides.body_md: Match each practice at a publishing house with the incentive it represents.
slides.narration: First decide whether each practice involves money. Then name the incentive.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: building an incentive package
slides.body_md: An imagined handloom cooperative faces four problems. Suggest one incentive for each.
bullets: Step 1 — Find the need behind each problem.
Step 2 — Money worries call for financial incentives.
Step 3 — Respect and voice call for non-financial incentives.

headers: Problem at the imagined handloom cooperative, Pochampally
rows: Weavers earn too little in the lean season
Old members worry about life after weaving
Their names on the sari labels
Young members feel they have no say
Seats on the cooperative's design panel

visual.alt: Worked example table for an imagined handloom cooperative: low lean-season income is met by a productivity-linked wage, worry about old age by a pension fund, unnoticed designers by their names on labels, and young members without a say by seats on the design panel

slides.narration: Look at the cooperative in Pochampally. Low lean-season income is a money problem, so a wage linked to finished saris helps. Worry about old age needs a pension fund. Designers who feel unnoticed want respect, so their names on the labels work well. Young members who feel unheard can be given seats on the design panel, which is participation.

slides.heading: Leadership and why it matters
slides.body_md: **Leadership** is the process of influencing people to work willingly towards group goals.

visual.alt: Table of the importance of leadership: it influences behaviour, builds relationships, introduces change, handles conflict and trains successors

slides.narration: Leadership is influence. A leader makes people want to do what needs doing. It matters because it shapes behaviour, builds relationships with followers, helps introduce change, settles conflicts before they grow, and trains people who can lead in future. A manager with formal authority but no leadership gets only grudging obedience.

slides.heading: Qualities of a good leader

rows: Earns the trust of the team
Acts without waiting to be told

visual.alt: Table of qualities of a good leader: knowledge, integrity, initiative, communication skill, self-confidence and decisiveness, and social and motivation skills, each with why it helps

slides.narration: What makes a good leader? Knowledge of the work, so that the team trusts the leader. Integrity, because people follow someone honest. Initiative, acting without waiting to be told. Good communication, including listening. Self-confidence and decisiveness, especially in difficult moments. And social and motivation skills, to understand and inspire people.

slides.heading: The communication process
slides.body_md: **Communication** is the exchange of facts, ideas, opinions or feelings between two or more people to create understanding.

visual.alt: Flow of the communication process: sender, encoding, message through media, decoding, receiver, and feedback to the sender; noise can disturb any step
visual.caption: Communication process (noise can disturb any step)

slides.narration: Communication has several elements. The sender has an idea and encodes it into words, symbols or gestures. The message travels through a medium such as speech, a letter or an email. The receiver decodes it into meaning and responds with feedback. Noise, anything that disturbs the message, can creep in at any stage.

slides.heading: Formal and informal communication
columns:
**Formal**

- Follows the official chain
- Slower, often written
- Reliable
- Networks: single chain, wheel, circular, free flow, inverted V

**Informal (grapevine)**

- Moves through social links
- Very fast
- May spread rumours
- Patterns: single strand, gossip, probability, cluster

rows: Single chain, wheel, circular, free flow, inverted V

visual.alt: Table comparing formal communication, which follows the official chain, is slower, reliable and has networks such as single chain, wheel, circular, free flow and inverted V, with informal communication, which moves through social links, is very fast, may carry rumours and follows gossip, cluster and other patterns

slides.narration: Formal communication follows official lines, for example a manager's circular to staff. It is slower but reliable and often recorded. Informal communication, the grapevine, travels through friendships and casual talk. It is very fast and can help managers sense moods, but it can also spread rumours. Wise managers use both channels.

visual.alt: Table of four barriers to communication: semantic from language and meaning, psychological from state of mind, organisational from structure and rules, and personal from attitudes of superiors and subordinates, each with an example

slides.narration: Messages often fail. Semantic barriers come from language: jargon, unclear words, poor translation. Psychological barriers come from the mind: distrust, poor attention, judging too early. Organisational barriers come from structure: too many levels, rigid rules, status gaps. Personal barriers come from attitudes, such as a boss who fears that ideas from below will weaken his authority.

sections.heading: 1. Meaning, characteristics and importance
sections.body_md:
**Directing** is the management function of instructing, guiding, motivating, leading and communicating with people so that they work towards organisational goals. Its four elements are **supervision, motivation, leadership and communication**.

**Characteristics:** it initiates action; it takes place at every level; it is a continuous process; it flows from top to bottom.

**Importance:** it starts action, integrates the efforts of many people, brings out their potential, helps people accept change, and gives stability and balance to the organisation.

key_terms.definition_md: Instructing, guiding, motivating, leading and communicating with people towards organisational goals.

sections.heading: 2. Principles of directing
sections.body_md:
1. **Maximum individual contribution**: techniques should draw out each person's full potential.
2. **Harmony of objectives**: personal and organisational goals should support each other.
3. **Unity of command**: each subordinate gets orders from one superior only.
4. **Appropriateness of direction technique**: the method must suit the people and the situation.
5. **Managerial communication**: orders must be clear and understood.
6. **Use of informal organisation**: work with informal groups, not against them.
7. **Leadership**: influence people without weakening their goodwill.
8. **Follow through**: check how instructions are carried out and help where needed.

sections.heading: 3. Supervision
sections.body_md:
**Supervision** is overseeing subordinates at work and guiding them so that work is done as planned. The supervisor is at the operational level, in daily contact with workers.

**Role and importance of the supervisor**
- Explains plans and instructions to workers.
- Guides and trains workers on the job.
- Maintains friendly relations and unity in the work group.
- Motivates workers and keeps up discipline.
- Passes workers' problems and ideas to management (the link between the two).
- Checks that work meets the expected quantity and quality.

An operational-level manager in direct contact with workers.

sections.heading: 4. Motivation and Maslow's need hierarchy
sections.body_md:
**Motive**: an inner urge. **Motivation**: the process of stirring people to act towards goals. **Motivator**: a tool used to motivate.

**Features:** an internal feeling; produces goal-directed behaviour; can be positive or negative; a complex process because people differ.

**Process:** unsatisfied need → tension → drive → search behaviour → need satisfied → tension reduced.

**Importance:** improves performance, changes negative attitudes, reduces turnover and absenteeism, and helps introduce change smoothly.

**Maslow's hierarchy** (lowest to highest): physiological, safety or security, affiliation or belonging, esteem, self-actualisation. **Assumptions:** behaviour depends on needs; needs are in an order; a satisfied need no longer motivates; a person moves up when the lower need is reasonably met.

key_terms.definition_md: The need for status, recognition and respect.
The urge to become everything one is capable of becoming.

sections.heading: 5. Financial and non-financial incentives
sections.body_md:
**Financial incentives** (money or money value): pay and allowances; productivity-linked wage incentives; bonus; profit sharing; co-partnership or stock options; retirement benefits such as provident fund, pension and gratuity; perquisites such as a car, housing or medical aid.

**Non-financial incentives**: status; organisational climate; career advancement opportunity; job enrichment; employee recognition programmes; job security; employee participation; employee empowerment.

Financial incentives mainly meet lower needs; non-financial incentives mainly meet higher needs, so a balanced package uses both.

sections.heading: 6. Leadership
sections.body_md:
**Leadership** is the process of influencing people to work willingly towards group goals.

**Importance:** influences behaviour; builds relationships with followers; helps introduce change; handles conflict; trains successors.

**Qualities of a good leader:** physical fitness, knowledge, integrity, initiative, communication skill, motivation skill, self-confidence, decisiveness and social skills.

**Styles**
- **Autocratic**: the leader decides alone and expects obedience; suits emergencies and unskilled groups.
- **Democratic or participative**: the leader consults the group before deciding; builds commitment.
- **Laissez-faire or free-rein**: the group decides; suits skilled, self-driven experts.

key_terms.definition_md: Influencing people to work willingly towards group goals.
A style in which the leader leaves decisions to a capable group.

sections.heading: 7. Communication
sections.body_md:
**Communication** is the exchange of facts, ideas, opinions or feelings to create common understanding.

**Elements:** sender, message, encoding, media, decoding, receiver, feedback, noise.

**Formal communication** follows the official chain (networks: single chain, wheel, circular, free flow, inverted V). **Informal communication** (grapevine) moves through social links; it is fast but may carry rumours.

**Barriers:** semantic (language, jargon, translation); psychological or emotional (distrust, inattention, premature judgement); organisational (levels, rigid rules, status); personal (fear of challenge to authority, lack of confidence in subordinates, no incentive to communicate).

**Improving communication:** clarify ideas; communicate to the receiver's needs; consult others; mind tone and language; listen; ensure feedback; follow up.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing that directing is done only by top managers: every level directs.
- Confusing esteem with self-actualisation, or safety with physiological needs.
- Classing perquisites or retirement benefits as non-financial: they are financial.
- Mixing semantic (language) with psychological (emotion) barriers.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark objective items: one correct option.
- Case parts: quote the line and name the principle, need, incentive, style or barrier.
- 3 marks: three distinct points; 5 marks: five points of about 20 words each.
- Differences: one basis per point, both sides.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best describes **directing** as a function of management?

options.text_md: Fixing objectives in advance and deciding how to achieve them
Instructing, guiding, motivating, leading and communicating with people so that they work towards the organisation's goals
Grouping jobs into departments and fixing reporting relationships
Measuring actual results and comparing them with set standards

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Instructing, guiding, motivating, leading and communicating with people so that they work towards the organisation's goals. Directing is the function that sets people in motion through instruction, guidance, motivation, leadership and communication. Fixing objectives in advance is planning, grouping jobs is organising, and comparing results with standards is controlling.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined tyre company in Chennai, the managing director guides the plant heads, the plant heads guide the supervisors, and the supervisors guide the machine operators. Which characteristic of directing does this show?

options.text_md: Directing flows from top to bottom only on paper
Directing is needed only at the operational level
Directing takes place at every level of management

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Directing takes place at every level of management. Every manager, from the managing director to the supervisor, directs the people below. This is the characteristic that directing takes place at every level (it is pervasive). "Initiates action" is a different characteristic, and the other two options are wrong.

questions.stem_md: Plans and the organisation structure exist on paper, but work actually begins only when managers instruct and guide people. Which characteristic of directing is described here?

options.text_md: Directing flows from top to bottom
Directing takes place at every level

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Directing initiates action. Directing is the function that sets the organisation in motion: it initiates action. The other options are true characteristics of directing but are not what the statement describes.

questions.stem_md: An imagined paint company in Nagpur found that its dealers' sales staff pushed only cheap paints because their commission was a fixed amount per tin. It changed the commission to a share of profit on each sale, so that staff gained most when the company gained most. Which principle of directing did it follow?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Harmony of objectives. The change brings the staff's personal goal (higher commission) in line with the company's goal (higher profit). That is harmony of objectives. Unity of command is about one boss, follow through about checking implementation, and informal organisation about using informal groups.

questions.stem_md: After explaining a new packing method to her team, the floor manager of an imagined spice unit in Guntur visits the packing line every morning for a week to see how it is going and to clear doubts. Which principle of directing is she following?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Follow through. Giving an order is not enough; the manager checks how it is carried out and helps where needed. This is follow through. The other principles are about getting the most from each person, choosing a suitable technique and clear communication.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined furniture showroom in Jaipur, the sales manager tells Rohit to stay at the billing counter, while the store manager tells him at the same time to arrange the new stock. Rohit does not know whom to obey. Which principle of directing has been violated?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Unity of command. A subordinate should receive instructions from only one superior. Rohit gets conflicting orders from two bosses, so unity of command is violated, which causes confusion and delay.

questions.stem_md: Before announcing new shift timings, the works manager of an imagined cement plant in Satna quietly talks to the workers who lead the plant's cricket club, so that they can explain the reasons to others over tea. Which principle of directing is he using?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Use of informal organisation. The manager uses the informal groups that exist within the formal structure to pass on information and win acceptance. That is the principle of using informal organisation.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Directing is a continuous process.

**Reason (R):** Directing goes on throughout the life of an organisation, whoever occupies the managerial positions.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: managers change, but the need to guide and motivate people never stops, so directing is continuous.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Only top-level managers perform the function of directing.
questions.solution_md: **False.** Every manager directs the people below him or her, from the chief executive down to the supervisor, so directing takes place at every level.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why directing is important for an organisation.
questions.solution_md: Any two points of importance (initiates action, integrates efforts, helps get maximum out of people, facilitates change, brings balance), each explained briefly.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It **initiates action**: plans are only ideas until managers guide people to start the work.
2. It **integrates efforts**: by guiding and motivating, managers make individual work add up to the common goals.

questions.stem_md: Explain the principles of "maximum individual contribution" and "harmony of objectives" in directing.
questions.solution_md: One correct explanation for each principle.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Maximum individual contribution:** directing techniques should draw out the **full potential** of every employee towards the firm's goals.
2. **Harmony of objectives:** the personal goals of employees (pay, growth) should be brought **in line with** the goals of the organisation, so that both are met together.

questions.stem_md: State three characteristics of directing.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct characteristics, each with a short explanation.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Initiates action:** it starts the actual work; other functions prepare the ground for it.
2. **Pervasive:** it is done by every manager at every level, wherever people work under a superior.
3. **Continuous and flows downward:** it goes on throughout the life of the firm, and instructions pass from superiors to subordinates.

questions.stem_md: Explain any five principles of directing, giving a short workplace illustration for each.
questions.solution_md: Any five principles, each named, explained and illustrated in a line.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Maximum individual contribution:** use techniques that bring out each person's best, e.g. matching tasks to skills.
2. **Harmony of objectives:** link personal goals to company goals, e.g. a commission tied to profit.
3. **Unity of command:** one boss for each employee, so orders never conflict.
4. **Appropriateness of direction technique:** choose the motivation or leadership method that suits the people and the situation.
5. **Follow through:** check how instructions are carried out and help where needed, e.g. daily visits after a new method is introduced.
(Also: managerial communication, use of informal organisation, leadership.)

questions.stem_md: Directing is called the heart of the management process. Explain five points of importance of directing in support of this view.
questions.solution_md: Five distinct points of importance, each explained in a line.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Initiates action:** people start working towards targets only when managers instruct and guide them.
2. **Integrates efforts:** it ties the work of many people and departments into one direction.
3. **Brings out potential:** motivation and leadership help employees use their full abilities.
4. **Facilitates change:** employees resist change; good communication and leadership help them accept it.
5. **Brings stability and balance:** effective direction keeps people working together smoothly, so the firm can grow steadily.

questions.stem_md: In directing, **supervision** mainly means

options.text_md: preparing the annual budget of the organisation
overseeing the work of subordinates and guiding them on the job so that it is done as planned
choosing the best candidate from many applicants
framing the long-term objectives of the business

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** overseeing the work of subordinates and guiding them on the job so that it is done as planned. Supervision is watching over work in progress and guiding the people doing it. Budgets and objectives belong to planning, and choosing candidates belongs to staffing.

questions.stem_md: Sushma, a supervisor at an imagined bicycle factory in Ludhiana, explains management's new safety rules to the workers and passes the workers' complaints about faulty gloves up to the plant manager. Which role of a supervisor does this show most clearly?

options.text_md: A link between management and workers
A guide who trains new workers
A planner of the company's long-term strategy
A recruiter of staff for the factory

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A link between management and workers. Sushma carries messages both ways: management's rules down and workers' problems up. This is the supervisor's role as a vital link between management and workers.

questions.stem_md: A new operator at an imagined printing press in Sivakasi cannot set the colour rollers. The shift supervisor stands with her for two days and shows her how to do it. Which function of a supervisor is being performed?

options.text_md: Training and guiding workers on the job
Approving the purchase of new machines

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Training and guiding workers on the job. Teaching a worker the right way to do a job at the workplace is on-the-job guidance and training, an important function of the supervisor.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A supervisor is in daily, direct contact with the workers.

**Reason (R):** A supervisor belongs to the top level of management.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: supervisors work alongside operatives every day. R is false: supervisors are at the lowest (operational) level of management, which is exactly why they are in direct contact with workers.

questions.stem_md: State two ways in which a good supervisor helps the workers under him or her.
questions.solution_md: Any two functions of a supervisor that help workers (guidance and training, motivation, maintaining group unity, feedback).

answer.model_answer_md:
1. He or she **guides and trains** workers on the job so that they learn the correct method.
2. He or she **builds team spirit** and keeps workers motivated, so that small groups work together smoothly.

questions.stem_md: Arjun is the supervisor of the loading bay at an imagined warehouse in Nashik. He tells workers about the new delivery targets, settles a quarrel between two loaders, and tells the manager that the conveyor belt needs repair. Identify three roles of a supervisor shown here.
questions.solution_md: Three roles, each tied to a line of the situation.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Communicating plans to workers:** he explains "the new delivery targets" to the team.
2. **Maintaining group harmony:** he "settles a quarrel between two loaders", which keeps the team united.
3. **Feedback to management (link):** he reports that the conveyor belt needs repair, passing problems from the floor upward.

questions.stem_md: The process of motivation begins with
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** an unsatisfied need. An unsatisfied need creates tension, which drives a person to act in a way that satisfies the need. Reward, behaviour and satisfaction come later in the process.

questions.stem_md: Kiran, a senior designer at an imagined jewellery firm in Thrissur, is well paid and feels secure. She now wants her name printed on the collections she designs and a seat at the design committee. Which need is she trying to satisfy?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Esteem need. Recognition, status and respect from others are esteem needs. Her pay (physiological) and security (safety) are already met, and she is not seeking friendship or belonging.

questions.stem_md: Workers at an imagined brick unit in Bareilly ask the owner for permanent appointment letters and a pension scheme rather than a one-time cash gift. Which need do these demands reflect?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Safety or security need. Job security and provision for old age protect workers against future uncertainty, which is the safety (security) need.

questions.stem_md: A new accountant at an imagined travel agency in Shillong feels lonely and is happiest on days the team eats lunch together and invites her to their weekend trek. Which need is most important to her now?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Affiliation or belonging need. The wish to be accepted, to belong to a group and to have friends at work is the affiliation (belonging) need.

questions.stem_md: Dr Rao, the respected head of research at an imagined seed company in Hyderabad, turns down a bigger title and asks instead to lead a difficult project to breed a drought-proof millet, saying she wants to see what she is truly capable of. Which need is driving her?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Self-actualisation need. The urge to become what one is capable of becoming and to realise one's full potential is self-actualisation, the highest need. She already has status (esteem) and refuses a bigger title.

questions.stem_md: Which one of the following is an **assumption** of Maslow's need hierarchy theory?

options.text_md: A need that has been satisfied no longer motivates; the next higher need becomes the motivator
All people are motivated only by money
Higher needs must be satisfied before lower needs
Needs do not affect people's behaviour at work

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A need that has been satisfied no longer motivates; the next higher need becomes the motivator. Maslow assumed that behaviour depends on needs, that needs follow a hierarchy from lower to higher, and that a satisfied need stops motivating so the next level takes over. The other options contradict the theory.

questions.stem_md: An imagined software firm in Pune offers its employees the right to buy the company's shares at a price lower than the market price. Which incentive is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Co-partnership or employee stock option. Offering shares at a lower price makes employees part-owners: co-partnership or employee stock option, a financial incentive. Profit sharing gives a share of profit, not shares; job enrichment is non-financial.

questions.stem_md: Instead of only fitting soles, workers at an imagined shoe unit in Kanpur are now given whole pairs to make, choose their own work order and check their own quality. Which non-financial incentive is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Job enrichment. Designing jobs with more variety, responsibility and scope for growth is job enrichment. Job security is about continuity of work, status about rank, and perquisites are financial.

questions.stem_md: Front-desk staff at an imagined hotel in Udaipur are told they may give a refund or a free room upgrade to an unhappy guest up to a set limit without asking the manager. Which non-financial incentive does this show?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Employee empowerment. Giving employees more autonomy and power to decide on the spot is employee empowerment. It makes them feel trusted and responsible for results.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is an example of **perquisites** offered to managers?

options.text_md: A certificate of merit at the annual function
A chance to take part in management decisions
A company car, free housing and medical facilities
A more challenging and varied job

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A company car, free housing and medical facilities. Perquisites (perks) are fringe benefits such as a car, housing or medical aid over and above salary; they are financial incentives. The other three are non-financial incentives.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A worker who cannot afford two meals a day is unlikely to be motivated by the offer of a grander job title.

**Reason (R):** According to Maslow, higher-level needs motivate only after the lower-level needs are reasonably satisfied.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A: the worker's physiological needs are still unmet, so an esteem reward (a title) has little pull until basic needs are satisfied.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Money is the only factor that motivates employees.

**Reason (R):** Financial incentives mainly help satisfy the lower-level needs of employees.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: recognition, job security, enriched jobs and participation also motivate. R is true: pay and allowances mainly meet physiological and safety needs, which is why non-financial incentives are needed for higher needs.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Employee recognition programmes can motivate workers even without extra pay.

**Reason (R):** Recognition satisfies the esteem needs of employees.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A: praise, awards and display of achievements meet the need for respect and status, so they motivate without money.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A bonus paid over and above wages is a financial incentive.
questions.solution_md: **True.** A bonus is extra money given over and above the wage, so it is a financial (monetary) incentive.

questions.stem_md: In Maslow's hierarchy, the need at the top, to become everything one is capable of becoming, is called the ___ need.
questions.solution_md: The highest need in the hierarchy is the self-actualisation need.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the needs in Maslow's hierarchy from the **lowest** to the **highest**.
questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (a) → (e) → (c) → (b). Basic physiological needs come first, then safety, then belonging, then esteem, and self-actualisation is at the top.

questions.stem_md: Match each practice at an imagined Kolkata publishing house with the incentive it represents.

options.text_md: Editors get a fixed share of the year's profit
Senior staff get rent-free flats near the office
The best proofreader's photo goes up on the notice board each month
Staff are promised that no one will be laid off this year

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). A share of profit is profit sharing and free flats are perquisites (both financial). A photo on the notice board is recognition and a no-layoff promise is job security (both non-financial).

questions.stem_md: State two features of motivation.
questions.solution_md: Any two features: internal feeling, produces goal-directed behaviour, positive or negative, complex process (individuals differ).

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Motivation is an **internal feeling**: it arises from a person's needs, wants and desires.
2. It can be **positive or negative**: rewards such as a raise, or fear of a penalty, can both push people to act.

questions.stem_md: An imagined bank in Bhopal gives its staff (i) a pension after retirement and (ii) a chance to sit on the committee that plans branch timings. Name each incentive and say whether it is financial or non-financial.
questions.solution_md: Name and classify each incentive correctly.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) A pension is a **retirement benefit**, a **financial** incentive because it gives money security after service ends.
(ii) Sitting on the timings committee is **employee participation**, a **non-financial** incentive because it involves staff in decisions.

questions.stem_md: Identify the need that each employee of an imagined dairy cooperative in Anand is trying to satisfy: (i) Bhavesh, a new milk collector, asks for an advance to pay his family's rent and food; (ii) Hetal, a veterinary officer, wants to be called "Senior Officer" after ten years of service; (iii) Mansi, a lab assistant, wants a permanent post instead of yearly contracts.
questions.solution_md: One need per person with a reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Physiological need**: Bhavesh is asking for money to pay for rent and food, which are basic needs for survival.
(ii) **Esteem need**: Hetal wants a senior title after ten years, which would bring her status and respect from others.
(iii) **Safety or security need**: Mansi wants a permanent post, which protects her against the loss of income when a yearly contract ends.

questions.stem_md: The salaries at an imagined call centre in Mohali are good, yet staff morale is low and many leave within a year. Suggest three non-financial incentives the management could use, with a reason for each.
questions.solution_md: Three suitable non-financial incentives, each with a reason linked to low morale or turnover.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Career advancement:** clear promotion paths from agent to team leader give staff a reason to stay.
2. **Employee recognition:** praising and rewarding good calls publicly meets the need for respect.
3. **Job enrichment or empowerment:** letting experienced agents solve complaints on their own makes the work less monotonous and more responsible.

questions.stem_md: Explain Maslow's need hierarchy theory. Also state how a manager can use it to motivate employees.
questions.solution_md: The five needs in order (two may be combined in one point) and the application of the theory by managers.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Physiological needs:** food, shelter and clothing, met at work through basic pay.
2. **Safety needs:** security of job and income, met by permanent jobs and pensions.
3. **Affiliation needs:** belonging and friendship, met by teamwork and a friendly climate.
4. **Esteem needs:** status and recognition; **self-actualisation:** reaching one's full potential through challenging work.
5. **Use for managers:** find the level each employee has reached and offer incentives for the **next unmet need**, since a satisfied need no longer motivates.

questions.stem_md: Explain any five non-financial incentives that a business can offer its employees.
questions.solution_md: Any five non-financial incentives, each named and explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Status:** a higher rank or title raises self-respect and standing in the firm.
2. **Organisational climate:** a friendly, trusting atmosphere with fair treatment makes people want to work.
3. **Career advancement:** chances of promotion with training encourage employees to improve.
4. **Employee recognition:** praise, awards or a mention at meetings meet the need for respect.
5. **Job security:** assurance of continued employment removes fear and lets people concentrate.
(Also: job enrichment, employee participation, employee empowerment.)

questions.stem_md: The owner of an imagined construction firm in Patna makes every decision himself, gives orders without explanation and expects workers to obey them exactly. Which leadership style is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Autocratic leadership. Keeping all decision power with the leader and expecting obedience is autocratic (authoritarian) leadership. Democratic and participative styles consult the group, and laissez-faire leaves decisions to the group.

questions.stem_md: Before choosing the theme of the annual sale, the manager of an imagined clothing store in Indore asks her team for ideas, discusses them openly and then decides with their views in mind. Which leadership style is she using?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Democratic or participative leadership. Consulting subordinates and taking their views into account before deciding is the democratic (participative) style.

questions.stem_md: The head of an imagined research lab in Bengaluru sets the broad goal for a team of highly qualified scientists and leaves them free to decide their own methods, stepping in only when asked. Which leadership style suits this description?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Laissez-faire or free-rein leadership. Giving a capable, self-driven group full freedom to decide while the leader only supports them is the laissez-faire (free-rein) style.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a quality of a good leader?

options.text_md: Initiative: taking the first step without waiting to be told

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Initiative: taking the first step without waiting to be told. Initiative is a key quality of a good leader, along with knowledge, integrity, communication skill, motivation skill, self-confidence, decisiveness and social skills. The other options describe poor leadership.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Leadership is the ability to influence the behaviour of people towards shared goals.

**Reason (R):** A good leader possesses qualities such as integrity and self-confidence.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but R does not explain A. A defines leadership as influence; R lists qualities of a good leader, which is a different point.

questions.stem_md: State any two qualities of a good leader.
questions.solution_md: Any two qualities (physical fitness, knowledge, integrity, initiative, communication skill, motivation skill, self-confidence, decisiveness, social skills) with a brief explanation.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Knowledge and competence:** a leader who knows the work well earns the trust of the team.
2. **Integrity:** honesty and fairness make people willing to follow the leader.

questions.stem_md: Suggest a suitable leadership style for each situation, with a reason: (i) a fire breaks out at an imagined chemical store and workers must be evacuated at once; (ii) a team of experienced architects is designing a new library; (iii) a school's teachers are planning the annual sports day.
questions.solution_md: One style per situation, each with a reason based on time, the ability of the group and the need for commitment.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Autocratic:** in an emergency there is no time for discussion, and clear orders save lives.
(ii) **Laissez-faire:** experienced, self-driven experts work best with freedom to use their judgement.
(iii) **Democratic:** teachers' ideas improve the plan and taking part makes them committed to it.

questions.stem_md: What is leadership? Explain four points that show its importance to an organisation.
questions.solution_md: Meaning plus four points of importance.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Leadership** is the process of influencing people to work willingly towards the goals of the group.
1. **Influences behaviour:** a good leader makes people give their best willingly.
2. **Builds relationships:** the leader keeps good personal ties with followers, which wins their cooperation.
3. **Introduces change:** people accept new methods more easily when a trusted leader explains them.
4. **Handles conflict and trains successors:** the leader settles disputes early and prepares capable people for future roles.

questions.stem_md: In the communication process, **feedback** is

options.text_md: the receiver's response that tells the sender how the message was understood
the channel through which a message travels
the conversion of a message into words or symbols
any disturbance that distorts the message

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the receiver's response that tells the sender how the message was understood. Feedback is the receiver's reply or reaction sent back to the sender. The channel is the medium, conversion into symbols is encoding, and disturbance is noise.

questions.stem_md: The IT head of an imagined grocery chain in Mysuru emails all store staff: "Clear the cache and re-sync the POS terminal with the cloud ERP." Most cashiers do not understand what to do. Which type of barrier is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Semantic barrier. Technical jargon that the receiver does not understand is a semantic (language) barrier. Psychological barriers come from emotions such as distrust, organisational ones from rules and structure, and personal ones from the attitudes of superiors or subordinates.

questions.stem_md: Communication that spreads among employees through friendships and casual talk, outside official channels, is called
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** grapevine (informal communication). Informal communication that moves through social relationships rather than the official chain is called the grapevine.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined government-style trading company in Shimla, a clerk's suggestion must pass through six levels of officers before it reaches the general manager, and by then it has been changed and delayed. Which kind of barrier is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Organisational barrier. Too many levels in the structure and rigid rules for passing messages are organisational barriers. Nothing in the case is about language or emotions.

questions.stem_md: A receiver reads a message and works out its meaning. This element of the communication process is called
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** decoding. Converting the symbols of a message back into meaning is decoding, done by the receiver. Encoding is done by the sender; noise is a disturbance; the medium is the channel.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined design studio in Goa, all five designers send their messages only to the studio head, who passes them on as needed; the designers do not talk to each other about work. Which formal communication network is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Wheel network. When all subordinates communicate through one central superior, the pattern is the wheel network. A single chain runs down levels one after another, a circle passes messages to neighbours, and in free flow everyone talks to everyone.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** News spreads very fast through the grapevine.

**Reason (R):** Grapevine communication strictly follows the formal chain of command.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: informal news moves quickly from person to person. R is false: the grapevine moves through social links and ignores the official chain, which is one reason it is fast.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Feedback from the receiver completes the communication process.
questions.solution_md: **True.** Feedback tells the sender whether the message was received and understood as intended, so it completes the cycle of communication.

questions.stem_md: Converting a message into words, symbols or gestures before sending it is called ___.
questions.solution_md: The sender converts the idea into symbols; this step is called encoding.

questions.stem_md: Match each communication problem at an imagined bus depot in Madurai with the type of barrier.

options.text_md: A notice in English is badly translated into Tamil and confuses drivers
A conductor ignores the depot manager's message because he distrusts him
A rule says all requests must be sent in writing through three officers
The depot manager fears that suggestions from staff will undermine his authority

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Faulty translation is semantic; distrust is psychological (emotional); rigid rules and levels are organisational; a superior's fear of losing authority is a personal barrier.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between formal and informal communication on any two bases.
questions.solution_md: Two bases, with both sides stated on each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Channel:** formal communication follows the **official chain of command**; informal communication moves through **social relationships** (grapevine).
2. **Speed and reliability:** formal communication is **slower but reliable** and often recorded; informal communication is **fast but may carry rumours**.

questions.stem_md: The chief engineer of an imagined water-pump factory in Rajkot tells assembly workers to "maintain a tolerance of plus or minus 0.02 mm on the impeller bore". The workers keep making mistakes. Identify the barrier and suggest one way to overcome it.
questions.solution_md: Name the barrier with a reason, then give one practical remedy.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Barrier:** a **semantic barrier**, because technical terms such as "tolerance" and "impeller bore" are not understood by the workers.
**Remedy:** use **simple language** the workers know and show the limit with a sample part or gauge, then ask questions to check understanding.

questions.stem_md: Suggest three measures a manager can take to improve communication in an organisation.
questions.solution_md: Any three measures, each with a short explanation.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Clarify ideas first:** be clear about what is to be said before saying it.
2. **Communicate to the receiver's needs:** use words and a medium the listener understands.
3. **Ensure proper feedback:** ask questions and invite replies to confirm that the message was understood. (Also: consult others, be a good listener, follow up.)

questions.stem_md: Explain the four categories of barriers to effective communication, giving one example of each from a workplace.
questions.solution_md: All four categories, each explained with a workplace example, and a concluding point.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Semantic barriers:** problems of language and meaning, e.g. jargon, badly expressed messages or poor translation.
2. **Psychological or emotional barriers:** the state of mind of sender or receiver, e.g. distrust, premature judgement or inattention.
3. **Organisational barriers:** arising from the structure and rules, e.g. too many levels, rigid rules or status gaps.
4. **Personal barriers:** attitudes of superiors and subordinates, e.g. fear of challenge to authority or lack of incentive to suggest.
5. **Effect:** each distorts or blocks the message, so managers must identify and remove them.

questions.stem_md: Read the account of Annapurna Bakers and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined bakery chain in Pune, written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** One superior per subordinate is unity of command.

**(b)** Checking implementation after giving instructions is follow through.

**(c) (i)** Two principles, each with a supporting line.

**OR (c) (ii)** Two harmful effects of violating unity of command.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Unity of command**: each baker now gets instructions from one superior only.

**(b)** "visited each kitchen every day for a week to see whether the recipes were followed and to help with problems".

**(c) (i)** 1. **Harmony of objectives:** "a bonus that grew with the company's monthly profit, so that bakers would gain when the chain did well".
2. **Use of informal organisation:** "spent time with the senior bakers who were popular among the staff, so that they would explain the changes".

**OR (c) (ii)** 1. **Wasted effort:** with conflicting orders, bakers may bake the wrong items, causing waste of material and time.
2. **Poor discipline and morale:** bakers cannot please both bosses, so they feel frustrated and responsibility becomes unclear.

questions.passage_md:
**Annapurna Bakers, Pune (imagined)**

Annapurna Bakers opened three new outlets this year. The production manager, Neha, noticed that bakers were confused because both she and the outlet managers were telling them what to bake each morning. She fixed a rule that bakers would take orders only from her. She also introduced a bonus that grew with the company's monthly profit, so that bakers would gain when the chain did well. After launching a new sugar-free range, Neha visited each kitchen every day for a week to see whether the recipes were followed and to help with problems. She also spent time with the senior bakers who were popular among the staff, so that they would explain the changes to others in their own way.

children.stem_md: Which principle of directing did Neha apply when she ruled that bakers would take orders only from her?
children.solution_md: One superior per subordinate is unity of command.

answer.model_answer_md: **Unity of command**: each baker now gets instructions from one superior only.

children.stem_md: Quote the line that shows the principle of follow through.
children.solution_md: Checking implementation after giving instructions is follow through.

answer.model_answer_md: "visited each kitchen every day for a week to see whether the recipes were followed and to help with problems".

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Identify two other principles of directing followed by Neha, quoting the lines.
children.solution_md: Two principles, each with a supporting line.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Harmony of objectives:** "a bonus that grew with the company's monthly profit, so that bakers would gain when the chain did well".
2. **Use of informal organisation:** "spent time with the senior bakers who were popular among the staff, so that they would explain the changes".

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Explain two ways in which the confusion before Neha's rule would have harmed Annapurna Bakers.
alternatives.solution_md: Two harmful effects of violating unity of command.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Wasted effort:** with conflicting orders, bakers may bake the wrong items, causing waste of material and time.
2. **Poor discipline and morale:** bakers cannot please both bosses, so they feel frustrated and responsibility becomes unclear.

questions.stem_md: Read the account of Rangrez Textiles and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined weaving unit in Surat, written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Food and shelter are physiological needs.

**(b)** Giving employees a share of profits is profit sharing.

**(c) (i)** Name each need and link it to Farida's action.

**OR (c) (ii)** Judgement with a reason based on the hierarchy.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Physiological needs**: wages "barely covered rent and food".

**(b)** **Profit sharing**.

**(c) (i)** 1. **Older weavers: safety (security) need**; met by starting a **provident fund**, which gives savings for old age.
2. **Designers: self-actualisation need**; met by giving them **charge of a new festive collection** that uses their full creative ability.

**OR (c) (ii)** Yes. According to Maslow, **lower needs must be met first**; most workers were still struggling for food and rent, so a higher wage addresses the most urgent need, while the designers, whose basic needs were met, could be motivated by **self-actualisation**.

questions.passage_md:
**Rangrez Textiles, Surat (imagined)**

After a year of high staff turnover, the owner Farida Mistry met her workers. Many young weavers said their wages barely covered rent and food. Older weavers said they feared being dropped when orders fell and wanted some savings for old age. The two best designers said they no longer felt challenged and wanted to create a full collection of their own. Farida raised the basic wage, started a provident fund for all, and gave the designers charge of a new festive collection that would carry their names. She also began giving a share of every year's profit to all staff.

children.stem_md: Which need of Maslow's hierarchy were the young weavers trying to satisfy?
children.solution_md: Food and shelter are physiological needs.

answer.model_answer_md: **Physiological needs**: wages "barely covered rent and food".

children.stem_md: Name the financial incentive shown by "a share of every year's profit to all staff".
children.solution_md: Giving employees a share of profits is profit sharing.

answer.model_answer_md: **Profit sharing**.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Identify the needs of the older weavers and of the two designers, and state how Farida met each.
children.solution_md: Name each need and link it to Farida's action.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Older weavers: safety (security) need**; met by starting a **provident fund**, which gives savings for old age.
2. **Designers: self-actualisation need**; met by giving them **charge of a new festive collection** that uses their full creative ability.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Farida first raised the basic wage before offering the designers their collection. Is this order sensible according to Maslow? Give a reason.
alternatives.solution_md: Judgement with a reason based on the hierarchy.

answer.model_answer_md: Yes. According to Maslow, **lower needs must be met first**; most workers were still struggling for food and rent, so a higher wage addresses the most urgent need, while the designers, whose basic needs were met, could be motivated by **self-actualisation**.

questions.stem_md: Read the account of Code Nirmaan and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined software firm in Bengaluru, written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** All decisions with the leader and obedience expected: autocratic.

**(b)** Freedom to the group with support on request: laissez-faire.

**(c) (i)** Name the style with evidence and give one advantage.

**OR (c) (ii)** One drawback linked to the case and one practical change.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Autocratic leadership**: he decides everything himself and does not allow questions.

**(b)** **Laissez-faire (free-rein):** "lets the engineers choose their own tools and schedules, and offers help only when they ask".

**(c) (i)** **Democratic (participative)**: he "invited ideas and then chose a plan that combined the best suggestions". **Advantage:** pooling the ideas of both teams produces a better solution and the staff are committed to carrying it out.

**OR (c) (ii)** **Drawback:** autocratic leadership shuts out the knowledge of agents who deal with customers, so useful ideas are lost and morale falls. **Change:** he could **consult agents** on rosters and reply formats, moving towards a democratic style while keeping final responsibility.

questions.passage_md:
**Code Nirmaan, Bengaluru (imagined)**

Code Nirmaan has two team leads. Vikram leads the support team. He decides every shift roster and every reply format himself and does not allow agents to question him; agents follow his instructions but rarely suggest improvements. Ananya leads the product team of senior engineers. She sets the quarter's goal, lets the engineers choose their own tools and schedules, and offers help only when they ask. When a major client threatened to leave after a server failure, the chief executive, Mr Iyer, called both teams together, explained the problem, invited ideas and then chose a plan that combined the best suggestions.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Which style did Mr Iyer use during the crisis? Give one advantage of this style for Code Nirmaan.
children.solution_md: Name the style with evidence and give one advantage.

answer.model_answer_md: **Democratic (participative)**: he "invited ideas and then chose a plan that combined the best suggestions". **Advantage:** pooling the ideas of both teams produces a better solution and the staff are committed to carrying it out.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Agents in Vikram's team "rarely suggest improvements". Explain one drawback of his style and suggest how he could change it.
alternatives.solution_md: One drawback linked to the case and one practical change.

answer.model_answer_md: **Drawback:** autocratic leadership shuts out the knowledge of agents who deal with customers, so useful ideas are lost and morale falls. **Change:** he could **consult agents** on rosters and reply formats, moving towards a democratic style while keeping final responsibility.

questions.stem_md: Read the account of the Tez Logistics depot and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined transport company in Lucknow, written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Language and jargon problems are semantic barriers.

**(b)** Structural levels and rules are organisational barriers.

**(c) (i)** Name the barrier with the line and give one suitable measure.
